top_evidence.document_title: Guideline-based and restricted fluid resuscitation strategy in sepsis patients with heart failure: A systematic review and meta-analysis
top_evidence.text: The meta-analysis was performed using the Review Manager 5.4 program (The Cochrane Collaboration, 2020) [9] by the random effects model with OR as the effect measure. The OR and 95% CI for mortality among HF patients with sepsis who received <30 × 3 vs. 30 × 3 were calculated for each study. The mortality data were totaled, and the studies were weighted to calculate a total OR and 95% CI (Fig. 2). The program calculated the I 2 statistic for heterogeneity analysis. I 2 estimates the proportion of variance that is due to heterogeneity. This metric denotes the proportion of variation throughout the included studies that is due to heterogeneity rather than chance [10,11]. The ProMeta program version 3.0 [12] was used to evaluate publication bias. This program generated a funnel plot (Fig. 3), and determined the degree of asymmetry using Egger's linear regression test and Begg and Mazumdar's rank correlation test (Fig. 4). [13] [14].

top_evidence.text: Table 1 shows an overview of the studies used for our meta-analysis . Kuttab et al. [15] found that a history of HF was associated with decreased odds of 30 × 3 (OR = 0.42; 95% CI = 0.29 - 0.60); this retrospective cohort study showed that failure to reach 30 × 3 was associated with increased odds of mortality (OR = 1.52; 95% CI = 1.03 - 2.24), delayed hypotension (OR = 1.42; 95% CI = 1.02 - 1.99), and increased intensive care unit (ICU) stay ( ∼ 2 d) ( β =2.0; 95% CI = 0.5 - 3.6) for patients with sepsis, without differential effects for ' at-risk ' groups including those with obesity, end-stage renal disease (ESRD), HF, or advanced age. One limitation mentioned is that the group with adequate fluid resuscitation had inherent differences compared with the other group, such as higher prevalence of septic shock, reduced time to antibiotics by ∼ 1 h, and likely increased recognition of sepsis with slightly higher rates of Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome and Quick SOFA scores on presentation. Uchel et al. [16] showed that although administration of 30 × 3 in HF patients with sepsis resulted in 2.5 times more intubations (23% vs. 9%; p <0.001), and 2.15 times more readmissions at 30 days (28% vs. 13%; p<0.001), HFpatients whoreceived <30× 3 had doubled the mortality (34% vs. 17%; p =0.0027). Taenzer et al. [17] used Medicare claims data to conduct a retrospective cohort study on the survival of elderly patients with severe sepsis or septic shock and a history of HF who did or did not reach 30 × 3 upon presenting to the emergency department. They used a proportional Cox hazard model to compare the two groups' 1-year survival rates and found that patients who received <30 × 3 had higher adjusted inhospital and post-discharge mortality rates (hazard ratio = 2.18; 95% CI = 1.2 - 4.0; p = 0.01). The weighted OR for death was significantly higher in the <30 × 3 vs. 30 × 3 (OR = 1.81, 95% CI = 1.13 - 2.89, p =0.01). Heterogeneity analysis resulted in an I 2 of 0% (Fig. 2), demonstrating a high degree of homogeneity among the results of the selected studies and pooled data. 30 × 3 is associated with lower mortality. Aside from the retrospective nature of their study, the number of patients analyzed and the small cohort of patients who received <30 × 3 limited their findings. Using Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services data, Rai et al. [18] , analyzed the association between receiving greater than versus <30 mL/kg fluid and in-hospital mortality (adjusting for age, sex, race, and Charlson score) in a subset of patients with a history of HF and sepsis. They found that the mortality was similar in those who received 30 × 3 vs. those who did not (OR = 0.91, 95% CI = 0.16 - 5.12, p = 0.914). They suggested that a larger cohort is required to support the benefit of 30 × 3 recommendation and its safety in patients with HF.

top_evidence.text: The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for case-control studies and retrospective cohorts was used by three authors (AW., AV., AC.) to assess the risk of bias in the included studies, all of which received a rating of >6 stars by each author (Supplemental Table 2,3,4). Publication bias analysis was performed by Egger's linear regression and Begg and Mazumdar's rank correlation test and displayed by funnel plot (Fig. 3). Egger's test revealed a p value of 0.95; and Begg and Mazumdar's rank test revealed a p value of 1.0, both suggesting no significant publication bias. This is visually demonstrated by a symmetric funnel plot.

top_evidence.text: The search yielded 26,069 records, which were reduced to 12,549 after removing duplicates. After removing records with irrelevant titles or abstracts, this decreased to 9 (Fig. 1). Of these, 2 were excluded because no clear timeframe for fluid administration was provided, and 3 others were excluded because no raw mortality data was provided. After assessment for risk of bias by three authors, 4 final studies were considered for analysis (Table 1).

top_evidence.document_title: Guideline-based and restricted fluid resuscitation strategy in sepsis patients with heart failure: A systematic review and meta-analysis
top_evidence.text: There is scant evidence to guide acute resuscitation of high-risk septic patients, such as those with a history of HF, and providers' adherence to sepsis bundles in HF patients remains variable. Earlier trials (Rivers, ProCESS, ARISE, and ProMISe) analyzed IV fluid as part of a comprehensive sepsis protocol. Therefore, assumptions based solely on IV fluid approaches in high-risk patients are limited. Confounders, on the other hand, would impact observational research based on retrospective data. There is a clinical debate about the optimal IV fluid resuscitation strategy. We merely evaluated the existing evidence by a metaanalysis approach. Based on the published research, our meta-analysis revealed that a restricted fluid resuscitation strategy (<30 mL/kg fluids within 3 h) in sepsis/septic shock patients with a history of HF was associated with increased risk of in-hospital mortality, while the included primary studies didn't achieve a statistical significance, except for the Taenzer et al. study. Our study highlights the need for extensive research to properly address the fluid resuscitation approach in this group of patients. Additional research in larger and more diverse populations may also consider the impact of HF with reduced ejection fraction and preserved ejection fraction phenotypes, the impact of pressors, the severity of sepsis, non-ICU sepsis admissions, and use of invasive hemodynamic monitoring to guide resuscitation.
